chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Yusuf from his father who said:

I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man from the Juhaynah tribe came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said: O Messenger of Allah, I am in the countryside with my family, my children, and my servants. I call the adhan, establish the iqamah, and lead them in prayer. Are we considered a congregation? He said: Yes. He said: O Messenger of Allah, the servants follow the drops of rain, so I remain with my family and children. I call the adhan, establish the iqamah, and lead them in prayer. Are we considered a congregation? He said: Yes. He said: O Messenger of Allah, my children scatter among the livestock, so I remain with my family. I call the adhan, establish the iqamah, and lead them in prayer. Are we considered a congregation? He said: Yes. He said: O Messenger of Allah, the wife goes for her needs, so I remain alone. I call the adhan and establish the iqamah. Am I a congregation? He said: Yes, the believer alone is a congregation.'

key_terms.اَلْمُؤْمِنُ وَحْدَهُ جَمَاعَة: The believer alone is a congregation

ai.seo_question: Is a single person praying considered a congregation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential definition of *jama'ah* by progressively removing companions until only the individual remains, affirming that 'the believer alone is a congregation.' This ruling alleviates the burden on travelers and rural dwellers, ensuring the validity of congregational prayer even in isolation. It underscores the Shia emphasis on the spiritual potency of the individual believer, linking physical solitude with communal spiritual status.
